title: What Makes a Leader Approachable?
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: The piece opens with the payoff side of high approachability and makes it concrete. Approachable leaders get the early reporting of issues, hear about problems before they escalate, and are asked for feedback and guidance in the conversations that actually shape decisions. Multiple studies, the authors note, have also shown higher engagement, productivity, and commitment from teams that perceive their leader as approachable. In large organisations the effect is a kind of compression: the place feels smaller and more collegial, not because the org chart changed but because the leadership status gap shrank. The mirror image is a sharp warning. Less approachable leaders are usually the last to learn about bad news, people in crisis, execution risks, and warning signs of discontent. They are caught by surprise by debates happening throughout the organisation without them, and they find out about resignations only after decisions have been made. The consequence is not just embarrassment; it is a real, compounding loss of information that the leader needs to be effective. The heart of the piece is the behavioural list, and the authors flag one move as the strongest single signal of approachability. Beyond seeking input on work issues, approachable leaders actively ask team members for advice on non-work matters: travel tips, restaurants, parenting, shows to watch, places to visit, technology to try. Doing so shows genuine curiosity about the person, admits that the leader does not hold all the answers even in trivial domains, and quietly makes them a whole human rather than a role. The close is a direct provocation. Some leaders deliberately choose unapproachability to feel powerful, and the price they pay is being excluded from the conversations where their effectiveness is actually made.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: High approachability shapes the relationship a leader has with team members in a profound and positive way. The more approachable a leader is perceived to be, the more likely they are to learn what others truly think and experience.

Approachable leaders get an early reporting of issues, hear of problems before they escalate, and get asked for their feedback and guidance. They are entrusted with knowing what bothers people and what adversities they face in and out of the workplace.

Multiple studies have also shown that team members who believe their leader is highly approachable display higher engagement, greater productivity, and increased commitment to the team. In large organizations, approachable leaders make the workplace feel smaller and more collegial by lowering the leadership status people perceive and by giving team members more access to what’s really happening in the organization.
Less approachable leaders don’t learn many things they later wish they had. They are usually the last to learn about bad news, people in crisis, execution risks, and the warning signs of discontent.

They amplify their approachability by showing visible interest in the work and lives of others, by listening patiently to what others say without defensiveness, by inviting challenge and inquiry from team members, by always treating people with respect and making them feel valued, by applying standards consistently and fairly, and by displaying an emotional evenness regardless of the issue or urgency involved.

In addition to seeking input as they think through issues and decisions, they also seek advice from team members on non-work and non-task issues. They ask people for travel tips, restaurant recommendations, parenting advice, the newest shows to watch, ways to recharge, places to visit, activities to experience, and technology to experiment with.

By consistently asking for such advice, listening intently to the response, and thanking people for what they have shared, leaders show themselves to be personable, open, and humble. This makes them safe to share any issue with.

Unapproachable leaders don’t learn what they need to, and their effectiveness suffers as a result. Too much distance is the enemy of great leadership.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
